Let \(F\) be the class of fibrations. For each level \(k=1,\dots,n\), define
\[
h(k)=\max\{i<k:\text{ some fibration }i\to j\text{ has }j\ge k\},
\]
with \(h(k)=-1\) if no fibration crosses level \(k\).

An arrow \(i\to j\) is a fibration exactly when
\[
h(k)\ge i\qquad (i<k\le j).
\]
Also \(0\to k\) is a cofibration exactly when \(h(k)=-1\). Hence
\[
c(\mathcal M)=1+\#\{k:h(k)=-1\}.
\]
Thus \(c=s\) means there are \(s-1\) gaps, splitting \([n]\) into \(s\) consecutive blocks. No fibration crosses a gap, and inside a block the maximum is obtained by making every internal arrow a fibration, except where forced by the prescribed value of \(f\).

Let the block sizes be
\[
a_1,\dots,a_s,\qquad a_1+\cdots+a_s=n+1,
\]
with the last block containing \(n\).

If \(r\ge2\), the last block must have size at least \(r\). For a last block of size \(m\), the maximum number of fibrations inside it with exactly \(r\) arrows into its top object is
\[
\binom{m+1}{2}-(m-r),
\]
because exactly \(m-r\) top arrows must be missing, and this bound is attained by deleting only those top arrows.

Writing
\[
t=n+2-r-s,
\]
the extra \(t\) objects beyond the minimum sizes must be placed to maximize a convex quadratic. For \(r\ge3\), all extras go in the last block. For \(r=2\), they may all go in the last block or all in one earlier block.

If \(r=1\), the last block must be a singleton, and all \(t\) extra objects go into one of the first \(s-1\) blocks.

Therefore
\[
\boxed{
A_{n;r,s}
=
s-1+\binom{r+t+1}{2}-t\,[r\ge2]
}
\]
and
\[
\boxed{
K_{n;r,s}
=
1+[t>0]\bigl((s-2)[r=1]+(s-1)[r=2]\bigr).
}
\]

So the requested ordered pair is
\[
\boxed{
\left(
s-1+\binom{r+t+1}{2}-t\,[r\ge2],
\;
1+[t>0]\bigl((s-2)[r=1]+(s-1)[r=2]\bigr)
\right)
}.
\]
